A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VAPT research despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison; rendered figures resolve text-extraction issues.

before.justification: v5 reports original VAPT classification, segmentation, sample-efficiency, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v6 retains those original results and adds PGD adversarial evaluations and image–text retrieval results in Appendices E.8 and E.10.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Equations (8)–(15) retain the same token-wise projectors, channel-wise convolution, shared feature projector, and adaptive-prompt construction. The new CLIP experiment applies this existing mechanism to its visual encoder without introducing a new VAPT component.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained classification and ADE20K segmentation coverage, v6 adds bidirectional image–text retrieval on ImageNet with natural-language descriptions and adversarially perturbed CIFAR-100 evaluation. These introduce a multimodal task and a distinct input condition.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated SA2VP, ViaPT, and VFPT comparisons. Table 2 adds E2VPT, ViaPT, and VFPT to the MAE/MoCo comparisons; E2VPT previously appeared only in other comparisons. These additions substantially strengthen the comparator set. The new retrieval experiment compares against the existing VPT baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E.10 introduces a CLIP ViT-B/32 retrieval protocol with 16 training examples per class, two training epochs, a frozen text encoder, the standard CLIP symmetric cross-entropy objective, and Recall@100 on 10,000 validation samples. Figure 8 introduces one- and ten-step PGD evaluations. Previously reported classification and segmentation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix E.8 adds a focused adversarial-robustness comparison on CIFAR-100 at two PGD step counts. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, backbone scaling, sample-efficiency analyses, and GradCAM examples remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report three initialization-seed runs and standard deviations for the classification results, together with the same one-tailed Wilcoxon tests in Appendix E.3 and Table 15. v6 introduces no additional uncertainty-estimation or repeated-run reporting practice for its new experiments.

E6.justification: Existing VAPT scores remain unchanged, including 72.91 VTAB mean accuracy in Table 1. Added SA2VP, ViaPT, and VFPT rows report 73.47, 73.70, and 73.20 respectively, changing the comparison rankings. New results include PGD accuracies of 22.41/13.37 for VAPT versus 17.33/11.87 for VPT at one/ten steps, and average retrieval Recall@100 of 80.19 versus 76.93 in Table 21.

T1.justification: Section 5 retains the same regression setup, estimator, Voronoi loss, and Theorem 1. Appendices A–B retain the same assumptions, Proposition 1, linear-activation theorem, and proofs. Changes there concern formatting, citations, and the appendix overview.

C1.justification: The abstract, four numbered contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims about adaptive prompt expressiveness, parameter efficiency, optimal sample efficiency, and the reported gains over full fine-tuning. The additional experiments do not redefine those core contributions.

C2.justification: v6 interprets retrieval gains as improved visual–text alignment and explicitly qualifies its PGD findings as preliminary, attributing degradation to limited data and absent adversarial training. Section 6.2 emphasizes conceptual value over achieving the best score everywhere. Section 4.2 also describes the unchanged theory more broadly as providing robustness and generalization guarantees.

D1.justification: The v6 abstract adds a repository link and states that code is public, although Appendix D retains its future-release wording. Appendix E.10 supplies retrieval implementation details, including prompt length 10, SGD learning rate 0.01, batch size 64, and one warmup epoch. Existing hardware and hyperparameter-search disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The expanded Novelty discussion and rewritten adaptive-prompting discussion substantially develop VAPT’s positioning against prompt-pool methods and MEPT’s explicit routing modules. New citations include ViaPT, VFPT, MEPT, and additional adaptive-prompting work. The earlier critique of input-modifying approaches is removed, together with the Pro-tuning reference.

P1.justification: v6 changes the title and affiliations, revises introductory passages, expands the novelty and related-work explanations, and adds reproducibility and language-model-use statements. The main section sequence and theoretical exposition remain largely intact, so the language and structural revision is localized.

P2.justification: v6 adopts ICLR formatting, expands Tables 1–2, adjusts their captions and emphasis, and adds PGD Figure 8 and retrieval Table 21. The existing GradCAM figure moves and becomes Figure 9. Other figures and tables retain their underlying displays despite resizing and relocation.

improvement.justification: The stronger comparisons in Tables 1–2 make VAPT’s performance–parameter tradeoff easier to assess, while Table 21 adds documented evidence for multimodal applicability and the abstract supplies code-access information. These are useful gains over v5. Their benefit is limited by retained state-of-the-art wording despite higher-scoring added baselines, and by the PGD experiment’s missing attack-budget details. The core method, proofs, and earlier results remain unchanged.
